author: Robert Goodman
title: Ray Bradbury (August 22, 1920 - June 5, 2012)
text:
Ray Bradbury (August 22, 1920 – June 5, 2012)
The Poet of Wonder and the Infinite Imagination
Although celebrated throughout the world as one of the twentieth century’s greatest writers of science fiction and fantasy, Ray Bradbury always insisted that he was, first and foremost, a poet. Whether writing of Mars, small-town Illinois, haunted carnivals, or distant futures, Bradbury approached language not as an engineer of speculative worlds but as a lyric artist seeking to awaken wonder. His fiction pulses with metaphor, rhythm, and sensory richness, blurring the boundaries between prose and poetry until each sentence seems to shimmer with the possibility of transcendence. To read Bradbury is to rediscover childhood’s capacity for astonishment while confronting adulthood’s deepest questions about memory, imagination, and what it means to be human.
Born in Waukegan, Illinois, Bradbury transformed the landscapes of his youth into the mythical Green Town, the setting for many of his most beloved works. His lifelong devotion to libraries (rather than universities) became the foundation of his education, leading him to proclaim that he had “graduated from the library.” That conviction shaped not only his career but his philosophy: books were living companions capable of expanding the soul, and literature was among humanity’s greatest safeguards against indifference, censorship, and forgetfulness. Works such as The Martian Chronicles, Something Wicked This Way Comes, and Fahrenheit 451 endure because they marry imaginative spectacle with profound human feeling.
While Bradbury is often grouped with science fiction writers, his true subject was never technology itself. Rockets, robots, and distant planets served merely as mirrors through which readers might better understand love, loneliness, mortality, and hope. His stories repeatedly remind us that the future is not determined by machines but by the moral imagination of those who build them. In this respect, Bradbury belongs as naturally among the great Romantic poets as among modern novelists, sharing with Blake, Shelley, and Whitman an abiding faith that imagination enlarges both the individual and civilization.
Less widely known, yet deeply revealing of his literary vision, are Bradbury’s poems. Written across decades, they possess the same exuberance, tenderness, and cosmic curiosity that characterize his fiction while stripping away narrative to reveal pure meditation. They celebrate childhood wonder, mourn humanity’s limitations, and rejoice in the endless desire to reach beyond ourselves. Bradbury understood that poetry, perhaps more than any other art, grants language permission to dream.
Among these works, “If Only We Had Taller Been” stands as one of his most moving reflections on aspiration. Borrowing its title from a line in Robert Browning’s Andrea del Sarto, the poem contemplates humanity’s eternal longing to exceed its grasp—not merely to conquer the stars, but to become worthy of them. Rather than lamenting our limitations, Bradbury transforms them into the very source of our greatness. The poem suggests that civilization advances because men and women continue reaching toward horizons forever beyond their immediate possession. In doing so, Bradbury offers a distinctly hopeful vision: our finest achievements arise not from perfection, but from our refusal to cease imagining what lies just beyond our reach.
Today, Bradbury’s voice continues to inspire readers because it reminds us that wonder is neither childish nor escapist. It is a discipline of the spirit, an act of courage that resists cynicism and insists that the universe remains larger, stranger, and more beautiful than we can yet comprehend.
Written late in Bradbury’s career, “If Only We Had Taller Been” is both a celebration of humanity’s cosmic ambition and a meditation on the creative impulse itself. Echoing Robert Browning’s famous assertion that “a man’s reach should exceed his grasp,” Bradbury imagines our species forever stretching toward the stars—not because we expect to possess them, but because reaching transforms us. The poem captures the optimism that lies at the heart of Bradbury’s work: that imagination is humanity’s greatest frontier, and wonder its most enduring inheritance.
"The fence we walked between the years Did bounce us serene. It was a place half in the sky where In the green of leaf and promising of peach We'd reach our hands to touch and almost touch the sky, If we could reach and touch, we said, ‘Twould teach us, not to, never to, be dead. We ached and almost touched that stuff; Our reach was never quite enough. If only we had taller been, And touched God's cuff, His hem, We would not have to go with them Who've gone before, Who, short as us, stood tall as they could stand And hoped by stretching, tall, that they might keep their land, Their home, their hearth, their flesh and soul. But they, like us, were standing in a hole. O, Thomas, will a Race one day stand really tall Across the Void, across the Universe and all? And, measured out with rocket fire, At last put Adam's finger forth As on the Sistine Ceiling, And God's hand come down the other way To measure man and find him Good, And Gift him with Forever's Day? I work for that. Short man, Large dream, I send my rockets forth between my ears, Hoping an inch of Good is worth a pound of years. Aching to hear a voice cry back along the universal Mall: We've reached Alpha Centauri! We're tall, O God, we're tall!" - Ray Bradbury, 'If Only Taller We Had Been'
If Only We Had Taller Been reminds us that poetry can inspire not only contemplation but aspiration. Bradbury’s language is luminous without becoming sentimental, transforming the night sky into both a literal and symbolic destination for the human spirit. Like much of his work, the poem suggests that our greatest triumphs are born from curiosity rather than certainty, and from hope rather than conquest. In an age often preoccupied with limits, Bradbury offers a timeless invitation to continue reaching—confident that the act of striving is itself one of humanity’s noblest achievements.

Submissions for both Featured Poet and General Poetry are now open for BY THE WAYE No. 04!
It’s that time again: submissions for By the WAYE No. 04 are now open!
For those of you who may not know, By the WAYE is a biannual print magazine of poetry and visual art published by WAYE Small Press and funded in part by a grant from the Jersey City Arts and Culture Trust Fund. Modeled after WAYE, the poetry reading series and open mic hosted at Sure Things since 2022, each issue of By the WAYE showcases a featured poet alongside other poets from the local community of New Jersey poets and beyond. Every issue also highlights the work of one visual artist.
We have two open calls, one for general poetry submissions and another for our featured poet spot for Issue 04. The featured poet will have between 15 and 20 poems in the issue and their collection will be flanked by the work of other poets whose work is selected for inclusion in Issue 04. You can submit work to both calls, but you will have to submit and pay separately.
Meet the Editorial Team for Issue 04
Please read the guidelines in full at Duosuma, Duotrope’s submission manager, and when you’re ready, send us your poemsThe deadline to submit is Sunday, September 6th, 2026.
